input.question: Why is it bad to reuse water bottles when unopened bottles can sit on the shelf indefinitely?
input.ground_truth: Manufacturing student here who works with plastics all the time. Most water bottles are made out of PET (poly ethylene terephthalate). Inherently, PET has nothing in it that could cause cancer etc, but the additives that the manufacturer uses can. They will add things like color, UV additives, fillers etc and these are the things that are actually harmful. BPA comes from only certain plastics like polycarbonate and PEEK (poly ether-ether ketone) and most companies will not uses these plastics in food or beverage containers. According to what I've learned, unless the plastic is melting in your food/drink, its generally safe and not "leeching chemicals" like everyone thinks. As far as bacteria goes, I don't know much about that to be honest

Question: Why is it bad to reuse water bottles when unopened bottles can sit on the shelf indefinitely?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a water bottle that you already opened and drank from. When you leave water in it for a long time, tiny germs (like the ones that can make you sick) can grow inside, even if you can’t see them. 

But if the bottle is still sealed and unopened, no germs can get inside because the cap keeps everything out. That’s why unopened bottles are safe to keep for a long time—they’re still clean and nothing can get in.

So, it’s not good to reuse a bottle you’ve already opened unless you clean it really, really well, because germs can hide inside. But a new, unopened bottle is like a clean, empty box—nothing has touched it yet!
